articles.title: Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup
articles.body:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia this morning, a company he co-founded in 1993. The decision came following the company’s board opening an investigation into multiple extramarital affairs Huang had with a direct report and an alleged Chinese spy. The new, and first, Chair of the Board, Harvey Jones, shared news of Huang’s resignation with the company in an email, which also announced CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.
Read Nvidia’s internal emails about the ‘extraordinarily difficult period’ amid CEO shakeup
Nvidia’s board and interim CEO Colette Kress told employees they’re ready to ‘move forward together.’
You can read the full text of the board’s internal memo and Kress’s first message to employees as interim CEO below.
Subject: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair
Dear NVIDIA Employees,
I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board.
As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA’s growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you.
Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence.
The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.
The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette’s leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.
Harvey Jones
Colette Kress’ first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO:
Subject: RE: Statement from NVIDIA Board Chair
Dear NVIDIAns,
I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy.
The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.
This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT.
We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let’s move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company.
Thank you for all you do,
Colette
Correction, November 12th: This story’s headline has been adjusted to better describe the context of Kress’ quote; she is not referring to a period “ahead,” as the headline initially stated.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after reports of extramarital relationships
articles.body:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected agent of China and another with an executive who reported to him — a stunning turn of events for the head of a company at the heart of the global AI investment boom.
Colette Kress, the company’s chief financial officer, will become interim CEO, Nvidia’s board said in a statement.
Nvidia shares plunged more as much as 16% after the board’s announcement, before later recovering and closing lower by 4.3%. A company spokesperson clarified that Huang will not be working with Nvidia in any capacity going forward.
The company also named its first chairman. That role will be filled by Harvey Jones, who is a former CEO of major chip company Synopsys. The addition of a chairman is a major governance overhaul at a company that for decades relied solely on Huang.
Nvidia’s board met Wednesday night to address Huang’s future at the company, a source familiar with the matter told NBC News, adding that the White House was aware of the meeting.
Huang, 63, co-founded Nvidia in the early 1990s and led the company’s meteoric rise amid the AI boom of the past several years.
“I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in her first email to Nvidia employees as interim CEO. “The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.”
In a separate note to the company’s workforce, Jones, the new chairman, wrote: “The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company.”
FOR SUBSCRIBERSNvidia is at the center of the AI economy. What happens now?
FOR SUBSCRIBERSHow suspected spy Alice Huang got involved with Nvidia’s CEO
FOR SUBSCRIBERSHow measles surged in the U.S.
FOR SUBSCRIBERSNvidia is at the center of the AI economy. What happens now?
FOR SUBSCRIBERSHow suspected spy Alice Huang got involved with Nvidia’s CEO
FOR SUBSCRIBERSHow measles surged in the U.S.
Kress has been the company’s chief financial officer since 2013. She is a familiar face to Wall Street, regularly appearing at conferences and discussing the intricacies of the company’s sprawling operations. Before Nvidia, Kress worked at Cisco, another major technology company, and Microsoft.
Huang long leaned on Kress during financial conferences and the company’s earnings calls to debrief the investing public about the latest developments with the company’s operations.
Nvidia’s board said that it would search for a permanent CEO and consider internal and external candidates.
President Donald Trump weighed in on the search for a permanent CEO shortly after Nvidia’s announcement, saying that Apple executive chair Tim Cook should take the role. “A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump wrote.
Cook only became Apple’s executive chair on Sept. 1 and did not appear to have plans to leave any time soon.
Kress’ ascension to the CEO role comes after the second largest public company in the world was hit with multiple scandals involving its founder.
On Wednesday, The New York Times, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, reported that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a married healthcare executive who reported to him, which appears to run afoul of Nvidia’s code of conduct. NBC News has not independently verified the claims.
Nvidia and the executive did not respond to multiple requests for comment Wednesday about the Times’ report.
The report concerning the alleged relationship followed reports that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, a businesswoman believed to be a spy for China. The two Huangs are not related.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated a memo to officials in the Trump administration this spring outlining how U.S. intelligence showed that Huang was in a romantic relationship with a business executive who was an asset of China’s spy service, according to a person familiar with Nvidia and a former national security official with knowledge of the matter. The New York Times and the Financial Times, citing people familiar with the matter, first reported on the memo last week.
Alice Huang held a senior position at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was buying advanced chips from Nvidia. Megaspeed and other related firms remain under U.S. criminal investigation of allegations they smuggled American-made chips into China.
Alice Huang’s precise role and relationship with China’s spy service is unclear. It is possible she was not a career spy for China’s spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, but was asked to cooperate and share information based on her access to Jensen Huang, according to the former national security official.
The concerns about the Nvidia CEO’s extramarital activity added to worries about Nvidia chips being smuggled or illegally accessed by Chinese AI companies. Nvidia has said that it follows U.S. export laws.
On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced it was investigating whether Huang had fallen victim to a foreign intelligence plot. It said Tuesday that it had hired a former acting U.S. attorney and his law firm to conduct the investigation.
Huang apologized in a memo to employees and said he supported the independent investigation.
“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Multiple Washington officials have called for greater scrutiny of Nvidia and for Huang to testify about his relationship with the suspected Chinese agent in the wake of the reports.
China has denied the allegations, calling them “purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China.”
Through Thursday’s closing bell report, Nvidia shares have plunged about 11% this week, wiping out $500 billion in value. Huang’s departure leaves a host of unknowns at the company, the valuation of which has soared to more than $4 trillion amid insatiable demand for its GPU chips. Those specialized processors underpin the AI applications that have powered the stock market and economic growth writ large to new heights.
For years, Huang has effectively been the chief ambassador for the artificial intelligence industry, appearing regularly alongside heads of state and other CEOs as the industry spends trillions of dollars investing and building AI models and data centers.
Nvidia acknowledged Huang’s contributions to the sector in its Thursday announcement. “Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound,” a statement said. “The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”
After coming up with the idea for Nvidia at a Denny’s restaurant in Silicon Valley with co-founders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem.
Before Wednesday’s report of a second affair, many high-profile figures across Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington had come to Huang’s defense. Trump told reporters Sunday that Huang had “done an amazing job for our country.”
“I think he’s an honorable guy,” Trump said. “I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”
Shaun Maguire, a partner at the venture capital group Sequoia, said on X that Huang is “one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” adding that “two mistakes don’t make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.”
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded under Maguire’s post, writing: “I agree.”
Before the decision, Musk said in a response to a post Wednesday night that it “would be an honor” to hire Huang.

articles.title: Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation into Suspected Spy's Company
articles.body:
Supported by
Singapore Says U.S. Not Helpful on Investigation Into Suspected Spy’s Company
In a statement, Singapore said it held Alice Huang’s passport months after President Trump was briefed that she was a spy.
Singapore’s government said on Thursday the United States had provided little help in its investigation into Alice Huang, the woman at the center of a spy plot that has led to the investigation of Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.
Singaporean authorities held Ms. Huang’s passport to prevent her from leaving the country from June 2025 until February over “potential false declarations” in relation to her company, Megaspeed, which is based in the country, the government said in a statement. She was ultimately released with a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore.
The statement raises new questions about the response of the Trump administration to the case and why the U.S. government did not more forcefully intervene. According to the timeline in the statement, Singaporean authorities had been holding Ms. Huang’s passport well after President Trump was briefed last fall about her relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive and the belief that she was a Chinese intelligence asset.
The New York Times has reported that Taiwan began monitoring Ms. Huang in 2024 at the guidance of the U.S. government.
In its statement, Singapore said that it had sought information from an American server maker and close Nvidia business partner, Supermicro, but that the company had provided “limited cooperation.” Supermicro, a firm that packages Nvidia’s A.I. chips onto servers that can be used in data centers, has been at the center of a number of chip smuggling investigations across the globe.
Supermicro was a supplier to Megaspeed, a company incorporated in Singapore and run by Ms. Huang, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.
Singapore said in the statement its authorities raised Supermicro’s “limited cooperation” with the U.S. Department of Justice and Federal Bureau of Investigation in July 2025 and “requested their assistance in securing the company’s cooperation.”
“Despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance in respect of the company,” the statement said.
Supermicro denied that Megaspeed had ever been a customer. “Supermicro did not sell any products to Megaspeed and has operated in compliance with all applicable U.S. export and re-export control laws,” the company said in a statement.
During questioning, Ms. Huang sought to downplay her role in Megaspeed, according to Singapore’s statement. She was ultimately released because of “insufficient evidence relating to the possible inaccurate declarations for which Megaspeed was being investigated.”
She was issued a “stern warning” and barred from re-entering Singapore. The country’s police are continuing to investigate Megaspeed.
Paul Mozur is the global technology correspondent for The Times, based in Taipei. Previously he wrote about technology and politics in Asia from Hong Kong, Shanghai and Seoul.

articles.title: Apple’s HomeView is my new favorite smart display — but not my daughter’s
articles.body:
The HomeView nails everything I want from a smart display. It’s superb at controlling my smart home; it’s an excellent hands-free kitchen companion, a good speaker, and a gorgeous digital photo frame. It’s also the first Apple smart speaker with Siri AI, which is an improvement, if still slow at times. But Apple has fallen into the trap that hampers other smart displays I’ve tested: Not content with doing its core functions well, it tries to do more, and that’s where the friction creeps in.
Apple’s HomeView is my new favorite smart display — but not my daughter’s
Apple’s first smart display is a gorgeous, speedy smart home hub and a great kitchen companion. It’s when it tries to be the family iPhone that things get awkward.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Got questions? Ask away.
We’re hosting a subscriber-exclusive AMA all about Apple’s HomeView today at 2PM ET. Drop questions here!
The special Apple sauce here is that HomeView is both a smart display everyone in your home can use and an extension of your iPhone or iPad, providing access to your texts, calendar, and reminders when your phone is at home and on the same Wi-Fi network. This makes it a communal device with personal data, and switching between the two is where HomeView stumbles. Clunky authentication checks and being sent to my iPhone too many times interrupt the hands-free experience. Not to mention that I could easily read my 15-year-old daughter’s text messages, and vice versa.
Her verdict? “I’ll just use my iPhone.” But my largely tech-averse husband fell in love with HomeView, and immediately asked for one for his office.
Apple HomeView
The Good
- Speedy smart home control
- Excellent guided cooking
- Siri AI is helpful in the home
- Gorgeous customizable faces
- Great sound for its size
The Bad
- I could read my daughter’s text messages
- Siri AI can be slow
- The app / widget situation is funky
- Wall mounts cost (a lot) extra
For households deep in the Apple ecosystem, especially those with younger kids who only need access to lights and music and aren’t interested in your text messages, this may be the first smart display your whole family will actually use. But for some, the idea of their texts appearing on a large screen in the middle of the kitchen will send them running.
Apple is late to the game here. Amazon and Google have had smart displays for close to a decade. But the company has debuted with a product that elevates the category in nearly every way — with a few quirks.
Polished and surprisingly small
The HomeView is much smaller than I expected, but it’s a great size for my needs. The star of the device is a 7-inch square touchscreen that displays a gorgeous collection of “faces” that I can customize to fit wherever I put it — the kitchen counter, bedside table, or the wall. It comes in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, and both cost $299, making it Apple’s least expensive screened device after the Apple Watch SE.
The tabletop HomeView fits neatly on my kitchen counter and is light enough to move around for cooking, or when my husband wants to check his schedule over breakfast. The long USB-C cable allows plenty of maneuverability, though after a few days of spinning, it did get a bit twisty.
The screen is clear and bright and looks good in most lighting situations. It’s large enough for reading messages, following a recipe, and video calling while in the kitchen. It’s super responsive, too, showing no lag or stuttering. There’s also a Center Stage camera above the display for taking a FaceTime call while moving around, staying in frame in every corner of my small kitchen. Callers could hear me clearly, although the farther away I was, the more tinny it started to sound.
Sound is very good for the size, with speakers on both the display and in the base of the tabletop model. It’s close to a HomePod Mini 2, not as room-filling, but with a touch more bass. Playing music on the wall-mounted model wasn’t as much of a downgrade as I expected in a device with one less speaker; it was richer and cleaner than on the Echo Show 15 wall-mounted in the same entryway. Siri responded well to voice commands using the device’s microphones, and as long as I remembered to put my phone face down if it was nearby, Siri replied from the correct device.
The one hardware miss is physical buttons; there aren’t any. When I want to adjust the volume quickly or mute Siri, I have to tap the display or pull out my phone.
I have a good spot on my kitchen counter for HomeView, but if you don’t, wall mounting is an option. Apple sent me two mounts for this review, both from Schneider Electric: a USB-C wall mount ($59.99) with a 2-meter / 6.5-foot cable and neat cable management, and a hardwired AC mount ($79.99). There will also be a power-over-Ethernet option for $129.99. The USB-C mount is easy to install: just two screws in the wall, then the display snaps on with magnets so strong that no one will accidentally knock it off the wall.
However, the wall-mounted HomeView ends up costing more than the tabletop version because it’s priced the same but doesn’t include a mount or a power adapter. You have to buy those separately, and with Apple’s $39 brick, you’re starting at around $400 (until the inevitable third-party options arrive). That’s an extra $100 for a device with fewer speakers. It’s a weird move; Apple should have included a wall mount and adapter or dropped the price.
Superb in the smart home
HomeView nails the smart display essentials: controlling my smart home, monitoring my video doorbell, providing hands-free help in the kitchen, playing music and podcasts, and displaying photos.
Apple put a Thread radio and Matter controller in the HomeView, so it acts as an Apple Home hub, the first with an always-on screen. The Home app is infused throughout the device’s software, giving you multiple ways to control connected smart lights, thermostats, locks, and cameras. This is where HomeView shines. It can connect to any HomeKit or compatible Matter smart device, and it’s impressively fast at controlling them, turning on the lights in my entryway as quickly as a regular light switch. It also offers tons of options for customizing its controls.
I set up the device’s Smart Home face with a large button to turn the lights on and off in the hallway it was in, plus smaller buttons for my Goodnight and Good Morning scenes, along with a live view of the Aqara video doorbell, and controls for my front door lock and Nest thermostat. In the morning, as I walk past, I hit the Good Morning scene and the house wakes up; then I do the reverse at night. Even better, my husband, who has never once opened the Home app, now turns on the lights from the HomeView every morning.
The Camera face, which streams up to nine HomeKit Secure Video cameras at once, is also very fast, and when someone rings the video doorbell, HomeView pulls up a live feed instantly. I can then unlock the door right from the display. I love that I can add multiple Smart Home and Camera faces in different configurations, giving me swipeable access to all the controls I want.
Smart home is my favorite use case, but I also loved cooking with HomeView. You can pull up a recipe on your phone and, using Handoff, send it to the HomeView, which brings up a guided cooking experience. This feature elicited several “Wow, that’s really cool” reactions from visitors (and my editor!).
It was easy to follow the on-screen steps while cooking, as well as use Siri AI for help. While viewing a Creamy Tuscan Chicken recipe, I tapped the cherry tomatoes and said, “Siri, what can I substitute for this?” It suggested some useful options and some not-so-good ones (cucumbers?). I also liked how the HomeView automatically inserted timers into steps like “Cook the chicken for about 8 minutes on each side.” Tapping the timers popped them up into Live Activities at the top of the screen, making it easy to switch back and forth between them and the recipe.
This switching with Live Activities also works for phone calls and music, two things I used HomeView for a lot. Answering a call on the large display while cooking is much easier than reaching for my iPhone, and the audio is loud and clear, so I could keep cooking while chatting from anywhere in the room.
Music and audio playback are great; it’s nice to see album art while blasting Taylor Swift, and the screen makes it easy to pause, skip, or navigate to a new song, album, or playlist. The built-in speaker is good, but I prefer to AirPlay to compatible speakers, and I like that the HomeView remembers which I used last so I don’t have to select them each time.
There are some disappointments. The HomeView has a built-in temperature and humidity sensor, like its HomePod siblings, but it can’t use its onboard 12MP camera as a motion sensor to trigger an automation. HomeView can also only control devices compatible with Apple Home, so that means no Ring doorbells or Nest cameras (without workarounds), or categories like lawnmowers or appliances that Apple Home doesn’t support. I also couldn’t get it to run some of the Siri shortcuts I use to have the voice assistant control unsupported devices. When I say “Hey Siri, feed Smokey” to any of my HomePods, they can trigger my Aqara pet feeder, but HomeView told me it couldn’t do that.
Apple Home still isn’t powerful enough for advanced home setups with complicated automations or a robust home energy management system; if that’s you, you’re probably already using Home Assistant or Homey and could bring your setup into a HomeView. Which you may want to do, because HomeView’s simple, intuitive interface is great for everyone else in your home. For example, my long-suffering spouse, who just wants a way to turn on the smart lights or adjust the thermostat without pulling out his phone, asking a smart speaker, or having me do it for him.
A little too personal
The other big promise of HomeView is to act as a family hub, with everyone’s personal data easily accessible on a communal device in the home while staying separate for privacy. HomeView uses face and voice recognition to show up to six household members their calendars, messages, and calls — in theory, only to them when they’re in the home. If you have an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, it can also answer personal context requests.
In practice, HomeView recognized me instantly, and I could swipe up from the home face to read my texts and access my calendar without any delay. But when it came to switching between profiles, it was too easy to access family members’ personal content. When I tested it with my teenage daughter, HomeView let me stay on her profile and scroll through her texts several times — even though it recognized me and popped up a prompt asking if I wanted to switch.
While this didn’t happen every time, it happened often enough to be a problem, mostly when I used the device right after her. There’s a grace period where the device stays on your content even after you’ve moved away; and if I hopped onto the device within five seconds or so of my daughter leaving, I could sometimes scroll for up to 10 seconds before it checked again and locked me out. (This was purely for testing purposes and with her consent!)
The other time we could reliably read each other’s content was when we were sitting side by side at the kitchen counter near the device. If my daughter was using it, walked away, and sat on the couch behind us, I could scroll through her messages for as long as I wanted because the camera still saw her in the room and didn’t switch to me, even though I was closer to it.
Swiping out of Messages to a face and leaving the room was the most reliable way to protect our stuff — but it wasn’t foolproof. (Watch my video review for more on this.)
I was impressed at how well HomeView switched between us on busy mornings. (Yes, my household does sometimes resemble that HomeView ad, minus the hole in the counter.) My daughter asked when her school project was due, then I jumped in to ask when to leave for the airport. HomeView answered each of us correctly, pulling from our respective calendars and texts — though we had to swivel the screen to face us, since it didn’t always recognize us by just voice. We could have used our phones, but HomeView’s large screen and louder speaker made hands-free use easier.
HomeView was stricter with phone calls than text messages, ringing only when I was directly in front of it. When my phone rang while I was on the other side of the counter, HomeView stayed silent until I spun it around.
This flow scuppers my hopes of using it as a family phone or putting it by my bed so I could banish my iPhone (and TikTok) to the living room at night. This is because it doesn’t show text notifications and won’t ring if it can’t see me, meaning I might miss a late-night call or text from my college-age son or teenage daughter.
Siri AI lands in the home
Tying all of these features together is Siri AI, which can answer general knowledge questions, control smart home devices, play music for you, and tap into personal context. I also didn’t have to repeat the wake word constantly; the Siri bubble animation on the screen clearly indicates when it’s still listening, so I could keep talking. Siri AI on the HomeView is an improvement over the older Siri on the HomePods, especially for controlling my home, and it’s mercifully much less verbose than its competitors. But it can be frustratingly slow to pull up personal context answers, sometimes makes mistakes, and regularly errors out. It is still in beta, so hopefully things will improve.
For smart home requests, Siri is very fast, since those run locally. It now responds to conversational requests like “dim the lights in here,” then “make it a bit dimmer,” making it easier to control devices. After it executes a voice command, it shows the accessory on the screen for additional control, which is handy.
I could also create automations with voice, such as “Hey Siri, open the shades in my office at 8AM every morning” and chain commands like “turn on the lights in here and in the mudroom.” But these only work with one device type at a time, so I couldn’t control lights and the shades with one ask.
I found Siri AI Personal Context handy in several instances, and it’s a feature that makes HomeView stand out from the competition — neither Alexa nor Google offers anything as deep. But here Siri can be slow, because it relies on pulling from your phone, and it struggles with anything taxing, like multiple requests in a row from different people. It frequently exclaims, “Uh oh, something’s wrong,” and gives up.
Then there was the time Siri tried to send my husband in the wrong direction. He asked it about his weekend schedule, and it read out the events in his calendar at the Georgia Bushcraft Fall Gathering he was heading to. When he asked how long it would take to get there, it confidently told him one hour and 47 minutes. He then asked it to show him directions, and it couldn’t because it didn’t actually know the address. Siri had guessed the location based on something in the event that said “Dogwood Stage,” and had made up the travel time. The gathering was actually a five-hour drive away. The event’s address was in his email, but Siri didn’t connect those dots.
When he prompted it to check his email, it found the correct address and calculated the drive time, but couldn’t pull up the route because there’s no Maps app on the HomeView. He asked it to send the route to his phone, and it said: “Done.” But all it sent him was a message with the drive time, no map attached. When he made the same request on his iPhone, it worked great. “It’s like your iPhone, but not as good” isn’t a great pitch here.
Despite these hiccups, I did find myself using Siri AI on HomeView a lot more than I do on my phone, where touch is my first and easiest instinct.
Beyond the basics
Beyond the core functions of a smart display, HomeView starts to struggle.
The built-in apps and widgets, which include Music, Calendar, Weather, Timers, Safari, and Intercom, work well. But if you want to use any other apps or widgets, they have to come from your phone, with some strange restrictions. They only work when your phone is at home, and only audio and video apps that support CarPlay and iPhone widgets that are compatible with the Mac show up. Because widgets point to apps that aren’t on the HomeView, they only work for glanceable info at best — tapping most of them gets you nowhere.
This means the New York Times and Apple News apps that appeared on the device were just podcast feeds, not news apps, and the Ring widget just told me to use my iPhone. A few of the widgets I tested offered some on-screen info, and some could perform one or two pre-programmed actions — there’s potential here, but it’s frustrating on day one. The only video app that works on the HomeView is Apple TV, but the screen is letterboxed to essentially iPhone size, so I wouldn’t recommend anyone buy this for a video-watching experience.
Safari is a workaround, and it’s not a terrible experience. I could browse websites by asking Siri to pull up The Verge or The New York Times in Safari, and I could log in to Netflix and YouTube using the pop-up keyboard. While I won’t be binge-watching the last season of Killing Eve on this, a Gordon Ramsay steak tutorial on YouTube while I cook, works fine but isn’t noticeably better than an iPhone.
There’s also no Maps or Notes app — and I felt their absence. A share sheet and the ability to copy and paste from Safari are also MIA, so sharing a grocery list or texting a link meant going back to my phone. HomeView made me do that a lot, which underscores how many features of this product are an extension of my iPhone rather than a standalone device.
How HomeView compares to the Echo Show and Nest Hub
I use and test all three major smart home platforms — Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and Apple Home. After a week with HomeView and Siri AI, I rank Alexa Plus as the best smart home assistant, Gemini for Home as the smartest assistant, and HomeView as the best smart display hardware and personal assistant.
Apple’s 7-inch square screen fits nicely into my home, and while it has similar dimensions to the Nest Hub, it has a smaller footprint. The Nest Hub Max, which launched in 2019, is showing its age and is significantly slower and laggier than HomeView.
The newer Echo Shows 8 and 11 are closer to HomeView in capabilities, but not as snappy. The just-announced Show 16 has a new UI with similar features to HomeView, but Amazon’s penchant for sticking ads on its smart displays has rightly put off many users. The HomeView has no ads.
When it comes to the AI inside, Alexa Plus is the most capable in the smart home. It can run multi-device, multi-room commands in seconds, and you can create complex automations with voice alone. Gemini can also handle more complex multi-step requests and is better with natural language and inferring intent from vaguer statements, like “I’m cold,” which will have it turn up the thermostat.
Where HomeView wins here is Personal Context. Google and Amazon offer similar profile switching, but neither is connected to your phone the way Siri AI is to your iPhone, so they have far less personal information to draw on. (Gemini for Home could certainly access much of it, but Google hasn’t gone there yet).
If Siri AI were a human personal assistant, I’d fire her for being too slow.
Of course, this is also a drawback: you need an iPhone or iPad to have a profile on HomeView. However, guests or visitors can use the smart home controls, timers, weather, Safari, music, and Siri for general knowledge.
Siri AI is also the only one of the three you don’t have to pay for to get the full voice assistant experience. Alexa Plus costs $20 a month or comes with Prime, and Google’s more advanced voice assistant, Gemini Live, is behind a paywall. Apple has said some Apple Intelligence features “are subject to daily usage limits,” with expanded access “available for a fee” in the future, but I didn’t run into any limits during my testing. However, Alexa Plus and Gemini Live are available on older smart speakers and displays; Siri is currently gated to the newest models.
Alexa and Google also support many more smart home devices; I can’t control my Bosch coffee machine in Apple Home, and my Ring doorbell and Nest floodlight camera don’t natively work with HomeView. Which is a shame, as HomeView is the best smart display for cameras I’ve tested. Ring devices work almost as well on an Echo Show, but Nest cams are slow on a Nest Hub, and third-party cameras struggle on both. The catch is only a handful of brands work with HomeKit Secure Video — including Aqara, Eve, and some Anker Eufy and TP-Link Tapo models. Apple’s own cameras, made with LG, arrive next year.
Apple is late, but pretty great
HomeView is a very good first smart display from Apple: powerful enough to run my smart home but simple enough for anyone in it to use. If you’re an Apple household and want it for any of its core jobs, you’ll be pleased, and at $299 it’s very competitively priced. But it’s not the full-fledged family organizer some households might want; Skylight’s Calendar still owns that niche.
For Apple Home users, the only question is how many do you want?
Where it gets complicated is when it tries to be your iPhone. Siri AI and Personal Context bring something no other smart display currently offers. But potentially seeing each other’s texts will be a deal-breaker for some. Too many tasks send you back to your phone, and if Siri AI were a human personal assistant, I’d probably fire her for being too slow.
This is all fixable: the option to turn off some personal features on the HomeView, a few more functional widgets and apps, and better options for displaying shared personal content like calendars could bring HomeView closer to the family computer I’d like it to be.
Today, HomeView offers enough for its price to be a good choice for anyone with an iPhone or iPad who is intrigued by any of its core features — particularly the smart home. For households already deeply invested in the Apple ecosystem and Apple Home, the only real question is how many are you going to buy?

articles.title: Who could replace Jensen Huang? A highly unscientific list of possible successors
articles.body:
It’s almost inconceivable that Nvidia would fire its rock star CEO. Yet here we are, on the precipice of this happening. Over at Kalshi, Jensen Huang’s odds of surviving the week are sitting at a lowly 30%. Even though he built one of the world’s most valuable — and, many would argue, dangerously powerful — companies, the tides have completely turned against him. He has confessed to an extramarital affair, but as of Wednesday afternoon it isn’t even clear who he meant: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive suspected by U.S. intelligence of spying for her country, or Kimberly Powell, an Nvidia executive who reports to him and who, five sources told The New York Times in an explosive new report, was also a paramour.
Even if Huang is pushed out as CEO, the board members he has made very rich are unlikely to cut him loose entirely. Barring another shoe dropping, they could keep him on as chairman, a role Nvidia doesn’t currently have. But someone still has to run the company, and there’s no apparent succession plan, which leaves us, like everyone else, to speculate while we wait to see what happens next. While Huang’s 60 direct reports undoubtedly get a closer look, consider this our own parlor game, featuring some obvious and less obvious candidates:
Lisa Su. The AMD CEO runs Nvidia’s most credible rival and is a distant cousin of Huang. The Information floated her name this week, but why would she leave her job for his? Her company stands to benefit from every day that Nvidia spends distracted by an investigation, congressional briefings, and all the mini dramas that are sure to follow. Her best move might be to send a nice note and keep her current corner office.
Eric Schmidt. He was the pick of Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management, who we talked with earlier this week. Schmidt could “parachute in tomorrow and do a very good job,” Sonnenfeld said, and perhaps he could. He ran Google from 2001 to 2011, chaired the National Security Commission on AI from 2018 to 2021, and now runs the rocket company Relativity Space. Chips, software, government, rockets — it’s an impressive range. Then again, Schmidt would bring a lot of baggage when it comes to his own extramarital dalliances. It’s hard to see him clearing the board for that reason.
Lip-Bu Tan. Intel’s CEO knows chips, and right now he might welcome a very soft landing. Last month, Intel reported third-quarter revenue up 21% to $16.5 billion, then warned its fourth-quarter results would fall short of Wall Street’s forecasts. The AI boom has caused a memory-chip shortage, pushing up PC prices and cutting PC sales. That’s hurt Intel (PC chips are a big part of its business), and its stock plunged 20% in after-hours trading on the warning, having already slid more than 30% since September. A move to a company that’s eating everyone’s lunch would be a pretty amazing escape hatch.
Bret Taylor. The former Salesforce co-CEO and OpenAI board chair now runs the AI startup Sierra, and his résumé includes a lot of the biggest brands in Silicon Valley. He co-created Google Maps, served as Facebook’s CTO, and chaired Twitter’s board through its sale to Elon Musk. He then took over as OpenAI’s board chair after the “Blip,” Sam Altman’s firing and fast return. When companies need an unflappable, likable adult in the room, they call Taylor. He probably knows nearly every customer Nvidia has, too.
Ian Buck. If the board feels strongly about having a “builder” at the helm, they could do worse than the Nvidia VP who helped develop CUDA, the chip software that has become central to Nvidia’s dominance in AI. Analysts and former employees have floated him as a possible successor, and Kalshi traders give him a middling shot. He’s no household name, but the Stanford PhD seems more viable if Huang can keep that chairman title and push for a successor he can work with.
Someone else down the hall. Andrew Bell, Nvidia’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, arrived 25 years ago as a fresh Cornell grad and has been on an upward trajectory at the company ever since. Like Buck and dozens of other executives who are presumably being scrutinized, he reports directly to Huang. Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is the insider most often named, but analysts say she isn’t necessarily a natural successor as an innovator and visionary, and Bell has the chip pedigree.
The wild card? Lori Huang. Nobody has floated her, but hear us out: Jensen met his wife as lab partners at Oregon State, so she has been working with him since before Nvidia existed. After graduating, she worked at Silicon Graphics as a microchip engineer (making more money than her husband, he has said), then scaled back to raise the couple’s family, and she now co-leads the family trusts. If the board wants continuity, they could do worse than a humbler Huang who is also a brainiac. There’s a reason they say that behind every great man is a great woman (and vice versa).
Whatever happens next, we’ll know soon.

articles.title: Here are the 25 original Xbox games you can now play on PC
articles.body:
For the 25th anniversary of Xbox, Microsoft is beginning to make good on its paid “next-gen game preservation” promise. Starting today, you can play 25 different original Xbox games on your Windows PC, as long as you have (or are willing to pay) for digital copies.
Here are the 25 original Xbox games you can now play on PC
Microsoft’s adding achievements to original Xbox games for the first time, too.
In July, Microsoft originally launched the idea with just four Xbox games, so 25 is progress, and Microsoft says all these games are now playable with keyboard and mouse.
Plus, Microsoft says it’s adding achievements to original Xbox games for the first time, starting with four games: Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and its sequel, Blinx: The Time Sweeper, and Conker: Live and Reloaded. You can unlock achievements playing them on Xbox One and Xbox Series consoles as well, after a system update. More games should get them in future.
Here’s the full list of Xbox on PC games, with the 21 new additions in bold:
- Armed and Dangerous
- Blinx: The Time Sweeper
- Conker: Live and Reloaded
- Crimson Skies: High Road to Revenge
- Disney’s Chicken Little
- The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind
- Fuzion Frenzy
- Grabbed by the Ghoulies
- Indiana Jones and the Emperor’s Tomb
- Red Faction II
- Secret Weapons Over Normandy
- Star Wars Battlefront
- Star Wars Battlefront II
- Star Wars Episode III: Revenge of the Sith
- Star Wars Jedi Knight: Jedi Academy
- Star Wars Jedi Knight II Jedi Outcast
- Star Wars: Jedi Starfighter
- Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic
- Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II – The Sith Lords
- Star Wars: Republic Commando
- Star Wars: Starfighter – Special Edition
- Star Wars: The Clone Wars
- Thrillville
- TimeSplitters 2
- TimeSplitters: Future Perfect
Yes, that’s a lot of Star Wars games, most of which already have a PC version, and few games that were exclusive to Xbox at the time. (But many of those Star Wars games were excellent.)
You also won’t be able to use an original Xbox disc to play these games, I’m afraid, as original Xbox (and Xbox 360) discs aren’t part of Microsoft’s disc-to-digital program; they predate the unique serial number that Microsoft embedded into Xbox One discs. In case you’re wondering, Xbox on PC backward compatibility appears to be powered by an emulator.
Also, most of the new games aren’t currently included with Xbox Game Pass, according to Microsoft; just Blinx, Conker, Crimson Skies, Fusion Frenzy, Morrowind, and Grabbed by the Ghoulies.
Leaked Microsoft documents previously showed us that October 2026 would be the “full launch” of original Xbox games on PC, while Xbox 360 games would have a “gradual” rollout to next-gen consoles between 2027 and 2028, which are when Microsoft is expected to roll out a handheld and a Helix box respectively. The way things are shaping up, the Xbox Helix should play games from every generation of Xbox, even if Helix fundamentally turns out to be a Windows PC.

articles.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
articles.body:
Explore our next generation products
Built for developers and teams in the agent-first era
Everything you need to stay up-to-date and get help
Gemini 4 Hydrogen and Orchestrator
Today, we’re rolling out Gemini 4 Hydrogen inside Google Antigravity alongside a new model dropdown option called Orchestrator, which pairs Hydrogen with Gemini 4 Carbon in an optimized balance of quality, efficiency, and latency.
Put Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen to work with Orchestrator
Earlier this week, we introduced Gemini 4 Carbon alongside /swarm for tackling massive, multi-worktree engineering tasks with parallel agent teams. In just a couple of days, tens of thousands of swarms have been launched on Antigravity, pushing frontier intelligence on the hardest problems.
For everyday feature work and debugging inside a single session, running a frontier reasoning model with multiple parallel agents on every step of every routine task slows down your loop and burns frontier quota. A common industry approach is to use a static “model router” that guesses task difficulty from your first prompt and routes the entire task to the cheapest model that is good enough to complete the task. Unfortunately, these start breaking down as agents become longer running, requiring different levels of complexity at different stages, often discovered as the task evolves.
Orchestrator takes a dynamic, bidirectional approach between Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen within the evolution of a single trajectory. For example, Carbon can start in a read-only phase to explore dependencies, resolve ambiguities, and build a concrete plan with explicit re-planning triggers. Hydrogen could then take over to write edits, update packages, and run tests. If Hydrogen hits friction, it would hand back to Carbon to inspect the state, repair the plan, and resume execution. This allows Orchestrator to reach near-Carbon task success while being faster and more quota-efficient. On Terminal-Bench 4.1, Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster.
- Explicit multi-model pipelines with the Antigravity SDK: When you want programmatic control over which model handles each role, you can wire Hydrogen and Carbon together directly with the Antigravity SDK. In the demo below, an open-source issue triage system built with the Antigravity SDK pairs multiple agents together. The Hydrogen agents handle triaging and coding to keep up with incoming issue volume, searching the codebase, asking clarifying questions, and fast UI iteration from PR comments while the Carbon agent is assigned to larger refactors, new features, and security checks.
- Fast, dependable execution with Gemini 4 Hydrogen: Hydrogen also works as a standalone model for everyday coding and agentic work, scoring 51 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (surpassing Argon’s 50, and reaching 54 at its highest setting) and 57% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 (more than tripiling 3.8 Flash’s 18.2%). When selecting Hydrogen directly, you can dial reasoning depth across four thinking levels, low, medium, high (default), and a new xhigh tier.
Getting started
Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings cutting-edge intelligence for everyday coding and agentic workflows. When you want frontier planning paired with speed without managing model switches, Orchestrator puts both Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen behind one prompt. Starting today, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is rolling out across paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. Orchestrator is rolling out for Google AI Ultra subscribers, with additional models and plans supported in the future. Enterprises can access both in Gemini for business.
