articles.title: I Accidentally Became a Millionaire
articles.body:
Yes, Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026 thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.
While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on November 7, 2026. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly $1,333,337 for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.
I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.
Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated1. Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.
Step 1: Making the million
The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).
Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.
Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the verifier, which is not actually supposed to happen.
Wait, what’s up with the verifier thing
So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer2. When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.
From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the VRP panel calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.
As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators can! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.
Okay so now you just give yourself the million?
Pretty much, yeah!
I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.
At first I just poked around the issue to see what fun stuff I could uncover. While doing that, I somehow managed to accidentally click on a sudden popup menu, which immediately assigned the issue to a bot account.
Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>
Accepted by yy...@google.com
Assignee:
yy...@google.com -> dx...@google.com
Status:
In Progress (Accepted) -> Assigned
Assignee:
dx...@google.com -> yy...@google.com
Status:
Assigned -> In Progress (Accepted)
Lyra Rebane <lyra.horse@gmail.com>
Marked as fixed.
vrp-reward:
1000 -> 1333337
Status:
In Progress (Accepted) -> Fixed
Realizing my cover had been blown, I decided to just go for it and set the vrp-reward value to $1333337, the largest bounty sum in the history of all Google VRP programs.
Step 2: Twitter
Having achieved my newfound wealth, I decided the next best step would be to announce it on the everything app3. I made my tweet in two parts - first, an announcement of achieving the record bounty, and then a video of me changing the vrp-reward value as the punchline.
Rebane@rebane2001 ·
my chrome vulnerability was just awarded the highest bounty in @GoogleVRP history - $1,333,337
Google VRP (Google Bug Hunters)@GoogleVRP
We ❤️ 🐜🐞🦗🦟🦋. {echo,{{{Google,Chrome,Android,Abuse,Mobile,OSS,Cloud}Vulnerability,Patch}Reward,VulnerabilityResearchGrants}Program}
0 Following44.3K FollowersAccount based in Switzerland?
jw
Followed by Jorian, Sijisu, and 75 others you follow
In just an hour, the joke tweet had already reached 600 likes. Since my intent was to just make a joke and not actually deceive anyone, and the tweet was clearly escaping containment, I followed it up with a clarification.
this is getting more attention that expected so just to be clear - the screenshot is real, i had mistakenly been given edit access and i used it to change the bounty field, but google did not assign this reward, nor will they pay it out to me. this was just for fun :)
Now, Twitter does actually have a feature to combat disinformation - Birdwatch (aka Community Notes) is a system that lets people add context to misleading posts. And this feature was in fact used on my tweet - in just a couple hours, the likes stopped rolling in, and this funky box appeared underneath.
Readers added context they thought people might want to know
Proposed by an experimental AI contributor responding to requests for a note. Like all contributors, AIs can make mistakes — verify accuracy.
Context is written by people who use X, and appears when rated helpful by others. Find out more.
And this would’ve been the end of it, if it wasn’t for the fact that Elon4 completely fucked up the Community Notes system! You see, this note here was generated by an “experimental AI contributor”, and thus, it claimed that I had “edited the screenshot [myself]”, which was simply not true!
This made me unhappy. And what do we do when we’re unhappy? We tweet about it5!
Rebane@rebane2001 ·
like its fair for this tweet to get community noted but could the community note at least be factual?
"the author edited the screenshot themselves as a joke"
no, the entire point of this post is that the screenshot is real, and the source in the cn literally states that
View quoted tweet
Rebane@rebane2001
a correct community note would read something like:
Google did not award an $1,333,337 bounty; the author was mistakenly given edit access to the bug and used it to change the vrp-reward field themselves
as it stands right now it makes it seem like i inspect elemented it or smth
And thus, pretty soon, the community note disappeared.
Step 3: Disinformation machines
From here on out, the tweet was picked up by an automatically generated AI news-podcast thing called Daily Vibe Casting, which describes itself as “A ten-minute daily roundup of what cracked 𝕏 in the last 24 hours.” Or in other words, it throws trending tweets into a chatbot.
Rebane reports a $1.33 million Chrome bounty
@rebane2001 says a Chrome vulnerability they6 discovered earned $1,333,337, which they describe as the largest award in Google’s Vulnerability Rewards Programme. The post does not explain the flaw, so there is little basis here for judging its scope or technical impact.
The payout is striking on its own. Browser security depends partly on researchers finding problems and reporting them, and an award this size puts a substantial price on that work.
Program: Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program (VRP) for Chrome
Previous Record: Historically, Google's top standard published tier for complex full-chain or sandbox escape exploits in Chrome capped out at $250,000 (such as the awards given to XBOW or individual researchers earlier in 2025/2026).
Would you like to know more about or details on other ?
AI responses will include mistakes. Learn morereward tiers
Lyra Rebane does not offer reward tiers. However, if she hypothetically owned a hotel chain, the reward tiers would be as follows.
Lyra Reward Tiers
Kibble: The kibble tier offers everything you need from a hotel, plus free juice box on arrival.
Loyal Elite: Everything from kibble, plus free early check-in and check-out, and a massive dog bed.
Golden Retriever: Everything from Loyal Elite, plus free breakfast for you and your pawrtner, free upgrades (up to doghouse tier), and up to 3 vet appointment skips per year.
However, this is just a hypothetical scenario and Lyra Rebane does not operate a hotel chain. Would you like to instead learn about or the ?
This text is an easter egg and thus not AI-generated.
security vulnerabilities
Sorry, I cannot assist you with this topic because you haven't passed our Hacker Reputation Test. To do the HRT, you must submit a list of CVEs you have been credited for.
Would you like me to tell you more about buying CVE accreditation, or do you want to learn about ?
This text is an easter egg and thus not AI-generated.
17 minutes ago — Researcher Rebane says the $1,333,337 payout is the largest in Google's Vulnerability Rewards Program. Daily Vibe Casting's Avatar.
And there it was! My little stunt turned into something that Google’s AI believes and makes into a story shown to every person searching for the highest Chrome bounty. And looking up my name now tells you about me being a millionaire!
There are a bunch of screenshots of this from other people under this thread. I’ve also seen cases of this affecting ChatGPT as well as Kagi Assistant.
Now what?
So that is the end of my fun little story. I doubt it was particularly surprising to anyone, but I think it’s a good case study on how both social media platforms and people’s reliance on AI can be abused to distribute disinformation and cause harm.
This example here, of course, is mostly harmless and just something that happened on accident - I wasn’t attempting to mislead people, and it’s not really my fault that Google’s AI didn’t read my replies in the Twitter thread.
One could argue that I’m a reputable security researcher with a track record of posting truthful information, so this is all moot anyways because I am trustworthy.
But I think this here demonstrates just how fragile and easily abusable our information channels are. If I was a threat actor looking to spread disinformation, how difficult would it be to pull something like this off intentionally?
Let’s play pretend
There are many ways to game Twitter. Its algorithm is publicly available, and people have figured out what kind of engagement results in what kind of algo boost. Bigger accounts can boost tweets and accounts significantly more7, so if you’ve got a few of those you can bootstrap new accounts way easier. But you can also just make bot accounts and slowly work your way up. And if you’ve got a bunch of accounts with reach you win.
And oh boy are there a lot of bot accounts! Look at, for example, the tweet this blogpost is about. There are a lot of obvious bot accounts in the replies. Maybe those very same accounts are also building reputation and voting on random community notes?
It’s kind of crazy to me that I could just post a tweet and have a community note removed. While the community note was actually wrong on a technicality, I’m sure there isn’t much preventing a bad actor from doing the same thing I did.
If I were a bad actor, I’d post disinformation that’s difficult to accurately disprove. If a community note doesn’t have a good source, or if it’s highly likely to get details wrong, it either won’t appear, or will have an easier time disappearing.
And all you really need to do is get a few tweets with specific keywords trending, and you’ve poisoned the search results, which then also poisons the AI.
And while you specifically might not take the AI Overview at face value, I’d guess that a lot of people do. It’s the first thing that shows up, it’s big and flashy, and it’s often unclear whether the only source of information is a tweet.
Tweets can mislead humans too, of course, but I feel like someone searching for something wouldn’t blindly trust a single tweet in the search results.
Note: While reading this post you may have tried to recreate the results I’ve shared, but without much success. The reason is that by now, my tweet has another community note on it, which Google picks up on and refers to the $1,333,337 bounty as a “prank”.
Also they took away my edit access and bounty :c
mi...@google.com <mi...@google.com>
Verifier:
lyra.horse@gmail.com (Lyra Rebane) -> <none>
vrp-reward:
1333337 -> 1000
afterword
heyyy!! been a while since the last post, soz
i hadn’t done css crimes for a while, so i wanted to get a new post out to get a chance to work on more of them again! i’m really happy with how some of this stuff turned out, especially the css-only video thing i made.
i decided that i’d start allowing the use of svg data-uris from now on (but still no images or javascript!). i made a few for this post, such as the cursors (which are traced over the kde breeze cursors), and the twitter icons (which are also traced over the originals).
here's all the svgs i made for this post btwclickingthesebuttonshasnoeffectexceptformakingthistexthereappearlol,butiguessthisalreadycountsasaneastereggsoknockyourselfout...

articles.title: AWS Lambda Web Functions keep billing memory ~7 minutes after the last request
articles.body:
Why we chose our own compute over AWS Lambda Web Functions
Lambda Web Functions kept billing memory for 5–7 minutes after the last request, so we built our own compute. On the same Next.js app, it answered warm requests 1.5–3× faster and cold-started about 3.5× faster.
When AWS announced Lambda Web Functions in October, I was excited.
At Easel, we'd spent months building infrastructure to run web applications efficiently on traditional Lambda. Native HTTP servers, concurrent requests, and active CPU billing sounded like exactly what we'd been looking for.
If Web Functions worked the way we hoped, we could potentially replace a substantial amount of our custom infrastructure.
So we decided to put them to the test.
A few weeks later, we'd decided to run our own compute instead. And as it turns out, our own infrastructure was faster, too.
The five-minute problem
Our initial experiments were promising. Web Functions handled 300 concurrent requests without errors, and a new function was serving requests in under nine seconds.
But we quickly ran into something that didn't work for us.
AWS documents that Web Functions bill for memory throughout an execution environment's lifetime, even when no requests are running. What the documentation doesn't specify is how long an idle environment will remain alive before being terminated.
In our tests, environments continued running and accruing memory charges for 5–7 minutes after their last request.
Across six representative environments, we measured idle periods of 313–411 seconds. There was no configurable idle timeout to shorten them.
For a 200ms request followed by 345 seconds of inactivity, that's roughly 1,700 times the request duration in metered memory time.
We checked the economics against CloudWatch and AWS Cost Explorer. Across our experiment, memory accounted for approximately 88% of the calculated compute and request costs at published list prices, even though our application only used around 160–210 MB.
The entire experiment amounted to about two cents at list prices. Hardly alarming on its own.
For an application receiving steady traffic, this may not matter much. The same environment can serve many requests, spreading the idle-memory cost across them.
But Easel needs to support thousands of applications with unpredictable traffic, including many that receive only a handful of requests per day. For those workloads, an environment might spend five minutes waiting for traffic after serving a request that took only a few milliseconds.
Multiply that across thousands of independent deployments, and the economics start to look very different.
We even tried terminating environments ourselves after 10 seconds of inactivity. That reduced metered environment time by roughly 20×, but AWS recorded every intentional exit as a runtime failure.
It wasn't something we wanted to rely on in production.
What if we ran the compute ourselves?
Rather than adopt Web Functions, we decided to move application execution onto servers we operate ourselves, keeping traditional Lambda available for overflow.
This gives us control over scheduling and resource allocation. We can share capacity across applications without paying AWS for each idle environment, and scale beyond our own infrastructure when demand requires it.
Our first self-operated compute host went live in US East on November 2, serving applications including Easel's own website.
But taking ownership of the compute raised another question: How would our performance compare to AWS?
We deployed the same Next.js 16 application to both platforms and ran a series of benchmarks from a client in Ashburn, Virginia.
The results surprised us.
Our host delivered 1.5–3× faster median warm-request times across all four workloads.
The difference wasn't limited to network or routing overhead. Running the same 20,000 chained SHA-256 operations took 29.2ms on our host versus 43.8ms on Web Functions, about 1.5× faster.
And cold starts told a similar story.
After leaving both applications idle for 12 minutes, we triggered fresh execution environments on each platform.
In both trials, Easel started serving requests about 3.5× faster.
We also saw an interesting difference after a shorter idle period. Following one five-minute gap, Web Functions had already terminated its environment and needed 908ms to respond. Easel resumed its paused environment and responded in just 14ms.
These are early results from a single region and a small application, not a comprehensive performance study. The cold-start comparison has only two paired samples, and we haven't benchmarked sustained throughput yet.
Still, seeing our own infrastructure outperform AWS across these initial workloads was encouraging.
Taking ownership of the infrastructure
Running our own compute comes with additional responsibilities. We have to manage capacity, handle failures, and make sure resources are distributed efficiently across applications.
But it also gives us the freedom to optimize the entire execution path, rather than working around the constraints of another platform.
Web Functions may be a good fit for applications with sustained traffic, where idle memory costs are less significant. For Easel, the economics of running large numbers of independent applications led us in a different direction.
And our initial benchmarks suggest that the decision doesn't have to come at the expense of performance.
We're taking on more infrastructure complexity so developers using Easel don't have to.
How we measured
- Dates
- Benchmarks ran November 11–12, 2026 (UTC). Idle-memory measurements are from October 26, 2026.
- Setup
- The same Next.js 16 application on Easel's self-operated US East host and on AWS Lambda Web Functions in us-east-1.
- Client
- One client in Ashburn, Virginia.
- Timing
- Time to first byte, excluding TLS connection setup but including network transit and platform routing.
- Samples
- About 100 requests per route per platform for warm requests. Two paired trials for cold starts.
- Hardware
- The platforms ran on different hardware and resource configurations, so these compare deployments, not normalized hardware.
- Pricing
- AWS costs use published list prices.

articles.title: Jensen Huang agrees to testify before Congress
articles.body:
Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress, House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said on Thursday, according to reports from Bloomberg and NBC News.
Huang, who stepped down as CEO following reports of an alleged affair with a woman suspected of spying for China, agreed to testify Wednesday after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress by Thanksgiving, which falls later this month.
The development comes after House Republicans Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford sent Huang a letter on November 4 requesting that he appear before their committees. Moolenaar chairs the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party, Mast chairs the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, and Crawford chairs the House Intelligence Committee.
“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony will take place behind closed doors, though Mast said he expects the briefing to be recorded on video and transcribed.

articles.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang Face Shareholder Lawsuit Alleging Investors Were Misled About Spy Affair
articles.body:
Nvidia and Jensen Huang Face Shareholder Lawsuit Alleging Investors Were Misled About Spy Affair (apnews.com) 10
			
		 	
				Charlotte Web shares a report from the Associated Press:  A shareholder has sued Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses to media reports about Huang's affair with a purported Chinese spy that threatens national security. [...] The news reports said that the Commerce Department was investigating Alice Huang's company, Singapore-based Megaspeed, on suspicions that it was helping to sidestep U.S. export restrictions blocking Nvidia chips from being sold to China. But Nvidia said then that its compliance team checked and determined that Megaspeed wasn't doing anything illegal.
But, according to the complaint, the statements were misleading because they were made when Jensen Huang was having an affair with Alice Huang, who is "suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products into China." It accuses Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia's relationship with Megaspeed, which posed a "material risk" to Nvidia's reputation and business prospects.
[...] "As a result of Defendants' wrongful acts and omissions, and the precipitous decline in the market value of the Company's securities, Plaintiff and other Class members have suffered significant losses and damages," the complaint said. Had investors known the truth, they wouldn't have purchased Nvidia's shares "at the artificially inflated prices that they did, or at all," the complaint said.  "Fun fact: Nvidia donated $25 million to Trump's White House ballroom fund," notes Slashdot reader Charlotte Web. 
UPDATE: The New York Times reports that Huang also also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company's vice president of health care and a direct report.

articles.title: Trump floats Apple chairman Tim Cook as Jensen Huang’s successor
articles.body:
In the wake of the industry-shaking news of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation on Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump is floating the idea that former Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over the position.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that “only one man” could take Huang’s place: Tim Cook of Apple.
“A Legend replaces a Legend!” he wrote.
Cook stepped down as Apple’s CEO on September 1, 2026, after 15 years running the company, but he’s still very much involved with Apple. While John Ternus took over as Apple’s CEO, Cook transitioned into the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors, which sees him continuing to engage with global policymakers and manage international relationships, including Apple’s relations with China.
Trump is not the only one to suggest Cook as a replacement for Huang. Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, Senior Associate Dean for Leadership Studies at Yale School of Management, who studies CEO leadership and corporate governance, penned an op-ed in Time on Wednesday, suggesting Cook should be among the potential candidates. He wrote that Cook has “an unparalleled track record of succeeding a bigger-than-life founder,” in reference to Cook taking over from Apple founder Steve Jobs.
Whether or not Trump agrees with this opinion, or is simply blasting off an idea that hopped into his mind, is anyone’s guess.
“Tim Nvidia,” however, doesn’t quite have the same ring as “Tim Apple” does.

articles.title: Researchers discover rare star system that emits radio signals every 8 minutes
articles.body:
Scientists at the Curtin University node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) have linked mysterious radio pulses to an unusual pairing of stars — a dead star that spins every eight minutes and a star similar to our own Sun.
The newly discovered system, known as GPM J071507−114153, consists of two stars orbiting each other: a white dwarf — the dense core left behind when a star dies — and a G-type star similar to our own Sun.
It is the first time radio pulses have been detected from a white dwarf orbiting a Sun-like star. Typically, such pulses are observed in systems with smaller and cooler red dwarf stars, meaning the discovery breaks new ground.
These types of stellar pairs belong to a broader class of objects known as long-period transients (LPTs), producing radio signals that switch on and off over intervals ranging from minutes to hours. Around a dozen have been detected since the first was discovered by the same ICRAR team in 2021, and astronomers are still working to understand them.
While several previously discovered LPT systems contain a white dwarf and another star, it has remained unclear which of the two stars was generating the radio pulses.
“This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself,” said lead author and commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, Dr Sam McSweeney, who made this discovery while working as a researcher at the Curtin University node of ICRAR. The team processed more than 100 hours of radio data at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre to validate and understand the white dwarf motion.
Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, co-author on the paper, said that the pulses emitted by the white dwarf allowed the team to detect stellar flares on the Sun-like star, similar to those that create aurorae here on Earth.
“As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a ‘stellar prominence’, which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star’s surface.”
“It’s amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.”
ICRAR researchers have been at the forefront of discovering these rare systems.
“We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position,” said Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.
After the LPT was located using the radio telescopes, the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island, confirmed its association with a G-type star through optical observations.
Both the MWA, led by Curtin University at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia, and MeerKAT, built and operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in the country’s North Cape province, serve as precursors for the SKA telescopes, SKA-Low in Australia and the SKA-Mid in South Africa, respectively.
Dr McSweeney said, “If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.”
This study, ‘A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion’, was published in Nature Astronomy.

articles.title: Rust 1.100
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Language
Compiler
Platform Support
- i686-pc-windows-gnu is now a tier 2 without host tools target
- Promote wasm32-wasip3 to Tier 2
- Add new Tier 3 target powerpc64-sony-ps3
Refer to Rust's platform support page for more information on Rust's tiered platform support.
Libraries
- Stabilize custom allocators
- Map ENOTSUP to ErrorKind::Unsupported
- Fix soundness issues in std::sys::pal::sgx::waitqueue::unsafe_list
Stabilized APIs
Cargo
- Introduced Cargo's own linting system: some Cargo warnings are now emitted as lints that users can control in the [lints.cargo] table. This includes a new built-in unused dependency check via the cargo::unused_dependencies lint. docs #17298
- Introduced minimum publish age configurations, also known as dependency cooldowns. When the relevant config is set, the resolver ignores versions published more recently than that, unless they are already in Cargo.lock. (RFC 3923) docs #17335
- cargo-install: now uses the existing lockfile in the .crate tarball by default. --locked in cargo install becomes a no-op. #17388
- Cargo now uses a new directory layout for intermediate build artifacts. Tools that inspect the build directory may need to use Cargo’s JSON messages to locate build artifacts instead of relying on the build directory layout. The layout is not a stable interface and is subject to change. (build cache doc) #17354
Rustdoc
Compatibility Notes
- Closures now more precisely capture variables used in if let. This may cause new errors
- Check dyn-compatibility of trait objects in more places
- Infallible is now a type alias to !
- The never type fallback was changed to ! on all editions
- box patterns are no longer syntactically allowed
- Report Query Cycle errors in more cases when computing the layout of enums with explicit discriminants
- Always escape grapheme extenders in str::escape_debug
- Make let-else respect macro_rules expr metavariable grouping
- Iterator::{min,max}(_by_key) changed which Ord methods they use. This cannot change behaviour (other than being potentially faster) for types correctly following the Ord rules, but may impact types with inconsistent trait implementations.
- Emit an error when trying to enable SSE/AVX on an x86 (32bit or 64bit) softfloat target
- Require windowed (and exception) for Xtensa ABI
- windows-gnullvm: always link libunwind statically
- From version 1.94 up to 1.100 a number of ARMv7-A hardfloat targets required the VFPv3-D32 FPU as a minimum, as they erroneously had the d32 feature in their baseline list of features. Breakage introduced as a result of correcting this can be fixed by passing -Ctarget-feature=+d32 to Rust.
- Change "Rust" ABI on x86 to use SSE registers if they are always-available for the current target
- Make the ambiguous_glob_imported_traits lint fire in slightly more cases
- Make +fix-cortex-a53-835769 a default feature for aarch64-unknown-fuchsia
- Some impls on Box have been generalised to arbitrary allocators, which may cause new type inference errors
- The standard library now uses Unicode version 18.0.0
- WASI SDK version was bumped from 33 to 34
- On ARM targets, -Ctarget-feature/-Ctarget-cpu values that would alter the ABI are rejected as hard errors now.

articles.title: Cyberattack on Fireworks AI allowed hackers to access Notion customers’ chat transcripts
articles.body:
A cyberattack at Fireworks AI has exposed some of its customers’ data, the company has confirmed. Fireworks AI, a platform that developers use to access and use open AI models, said an attacker breached its cloud provider to gain access to a Fireworks development system, which allowed access to some of its customers’ data.
The company said in its latest security advisory that the cybercriminals took Fireworks’ customers’ billing information and some datasets. Fireworks touts tens of thousands of customers worldwide using its platform, including legal tech company Harvey and AI company Cursor.
At least one confirmed affected customer is online document editor and notetaker Notion, which said in a disclosure that the breach affected around 1% of its own customers.
Notion said that Fireworks alerted the company to a security incident and later confirmed that the hackers had stolen some Notion customer data. On November 3, Notion said it disconnected its systems from Fireworks, deleted the data stored in its systems, and stopped all connectivity between the two.
Notion confirmed this week that the hackers took chat transcripts of its Notion AI customers who used the “Insights” feature. The company said that the transcripts include “any input to or output from the model that was written to the chat,” but added that much of the data was unattributable and could not be determined from which customer it was obtained.
The breach at Fireworks AI shows how tech companies are reliant on other tech providers for their own offerings, and how cyberattacks can, as a result, spill over into other customers.
Fireworks said that it believes the hackers are financially motivated and that their goals are focused on selling tokens from breaching access to large language models, or LLMs. These schemes rely on selling to unauthorized third parties, who can burn through AI model usage without using their own resources.
This is the second breach affecting Fireworks in as many months, following a security incident in October.

articles.title: 💧 This Museum Has Standards
articles.body:
Variety recently had two related, but very different, headlines about the despicable Russell Brand. First, I saw this:
Russell Brand’s Instagram Account Removed By Meta After Rape Conviction
Sure, OK. Terminating the social media accounts of convicted felons is probably a good practice.1
Then there was this:
Russell Brand’s Pubic Hair Removed From London Museum After Rape Conviction
Oh. Uh…I suppose taking the pubic hair of convicted felons off display is probably also a good practice?
Viktor Wynd, the eccentric collector behind the Viktor Wynd Museum of Curiosities, Fine Art & UnNatural History in Hackney, confirmed that he removed the unusual artifact from his collection in the wake of Brand’s legal troubles.
“I took them straight off display and have no desire to hear his name again – he has no place in my museum of horrors,” Wynd told Variety on Wednesday afternoon. “My museum is full of disgusting things but even I have limits.”
Anyhow, speaking of The Onion, they really nailed it.

articles.title: United Airlines Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights On Behalf of Travelers
articles.body:
United Airlines Bans AI Agents From Booking Flights On Behalf of Travelers 64
			
		 	
				United Airlines is banning unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking flights, checking in passengers or making account changes on travelers' behalf. CBS News reports:  To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."
The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances. "As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access -- directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators -- to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.  "United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

articles.title: Modern Web Guidance 1.0: The web platform expertise your coding agent is missing
articles.body:
Published: November 10, 2026
In this new era of agentic web development, developers expect their coding agents to be experts at building for the web. And while the latest frontier coding models are quite capable and can usually produce something that works, if you ask a web development expert to review the AI-generated code, they can almost always find ways to make the code faster, more accessible, or more secure.
Chrome is investing heavily in the future of agentic web development, and to address this challenge, we introduced an early preview of Modern Web Guidance at Google I/O in May. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents.
Today we're excited to announce the stable release of Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, which includes:
- New modernization workflow that scans your existing codebase to help your agent find opportunities to safely modernize.
- Expanded guide database targeting hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps with expert-vetted, cross-browser solutions.
- Deeper human expert review for every guide, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review on our user-facing guides.
- Full evaluation coverage across all of our guides with a public eval dashboard showing the measurable improvements compared to agents without Modern Web Guidance.
With version 1.0, we're also excited to share that Modern Web Guidance is becoming a cross-browser effort, with Firefox and Edge joining Chrome to support, improve cross-browser compatibility, and contribute to the project. Building on our shared work with Baseline, our goal is to ensure that anyone coding with an agent can take full advantage of the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.
Regardless of what models or agent harnesses you're using, if you're building for the web, Modern Web Guidance belongs in your agentic workflow.
To install Modern Web Guidance, run this command from your project directory:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
Or if you already installed an earlier version, you can update to 1.0 by running:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest update
For additional installation instructions or to learn more, check out the Modern Web Guidance documentation, or watch this video for a brief overview:
Why developers and businesses should use Modern Web Guidance
It's undeniable that coding agents have helped developers write code faster than ever before. But in a world where everyone is using coding agents, speed is no longer a competitive advantage.
These days, it's more important than ever to differentiate on fundamental factors like usability and quality of experience. Here are a few ways Modern Web Guidance can help:
Reinforce best practices that models often miss
While frontier coding models do have a good grasp on many best practices, our evals show that there are still a number of important areas where they fall short, such as:
- Accessibility: Keyboard focus and inert management, reduced-motion support, and accessible form validation.
- User experience: Swipe and touch gestures, dialog and popover transitions, and light/dark theme implementations.
- Performance: Main-thread task scheduling, offscreen rendering isolation, and layout shift prevention.
- Security: Safe HTML sanitization, strict Content Security Policies, and passkey credential management.
Accessibility best practices are particularly important to get right because mistakes like bad ARIA can make a page less accessible than no ARIA at all. For version 1.0, our user-facing guides were reviewed and tested with real assistive technologies by accessibility experts who rely on them every day.
For a deeper look at the specific mistakes models make in each of these areas, read Top 10 things AI gets wrong in web development.
Use the best web feature for the job
AI models are very good at figuring out how to make something work with JavaScript, but in many cases, there are HTML or CSS features that can do the same thing with much less code. And since they're handled by the browser, they usually perform better and come with accessibility affordances. For example:
- Features to animate popovers and dialogs
- Features to enhance scroll- and swipe-based interactions
- Better APIs for smooth and fluid page transitions
New features can also improve the experience of a site in ways that matter to users. For example:
- Passkeys and WebAuthn: For faster and more secure login experiences
- Autofill: To improve checkout flows (especially on mobile) that often fail when using custom JavaScript-based form controls
Modern Web Guidance is designed to recommend the best feature for the job, based on your browser support requirements. Its guides have embedded Baseline and browser compatibility data, so it can tailor its recommendations to your project's needs.
Scan your codebase and find opportunities to modernize
Most web development doesn't happen in brand-new projects. It happens in existing codebases that have accumulated years of outdated workarounds, unnecessary dependencies, and polyfills that are no longer needed.
Version 1.0 adds a new modernization workflow that can analyze your existing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and package.json to find opportunities to safely upgrade, and then guide your agent through the changes.
/modern-web-guidance Modernize the code in this directory
In this first release, the modernization workflow uses static analysis to check for a limited set of patterns. We chose to start with a narrow scope that yields predictable results, and then expand from there. Over time, we plan to cover many more areas, including agentic audits where your agent reasons about your code directly instead of just matching known patterns.
Stay up to date as the web platform evolves
The web platform is a moving target. New features ship in browsers every milestone, and existing features that you perhaps couldn't use before are becoming Baseline with each new browser release.
Since Modern Web Guidance is built on top of Baseline compatibility data, and its recommendations are maintained by browser engineers, web standards experts, and accessibility specialists, these recommendations evolve along with the platform itself, and now your project can too.
Learn about new web features and best practices
While Modern Web Guidance is primarily built as a tool for agents, one thing we've heard from many developers is that they've actually found the guidance to be quite useful on its own—as a learning resource.
Even in this era of agentic coding, there's still value in building up domain expertise. And Modern Web Guidance can help you do that: either by reading the guides themselves, or using the CLI to search use cases and discover new techniques that may be relevant to your project.
Pair Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents
In agentic web development, authoring code is only one part of the workflow. You also need to run that code to ensure it works as expected. This is why we recommend developers use Modern Web Guidance along with Chrome DevTools for agents.
- Modern Web Guidance gives your agent the up-front expertise needed to write code following modern best practices.
- Chrome DevTools for agents gives your agent runtime visibility so it can verify, debug, and optimize that code across a wide range of device capabilities, user preferences, and network conditions.
Together these help your agent arrive at a better solution in fewer turns. Next are a few examples of how you can use these tools together to maximize effectiveness:
Optimize until you hit your performance target
Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to effectively break up long-running JavaScript tasks that block the main thread, but it can't test your code to see how long those JavaScript tasks actually block the main thread for.
With Chrome DevTools for agents, you can run a performance trace on a simulated low-end CPU to see whether or not you have a problem, and then use the performance advice from Modern Web Guidance to iterate until your code never blocks the main thread for more than 50 milliseconds (so it doesn't contribute to poor INP).
Test and refine your animations
Modern Web Guidance can show your agent how to properly and performantly animate features like modal dialogs, tooltips, and popover menus, but even with this guidance you still need to verify that the animations actually work and look good when used in the context of your full application.
Chrome DevTools for agents can run your code, interact with the page, and take a screen recording of the animation in action. It can then study the recording to ensure both that the animation runs and that it fits the style and feel of the rest of the site.
You can also use Chrome DevTools for agents to verify that when prefers-reduced-motion is set, the component honors the user's preferences.
Cache views without memory leaks
Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to make SPA transitions feel instant by rendering and caching views in memory, while also properly hiding them from the accessibility tree.
However, when doing this it's important to ensure you properly clean up unused views to not leak memory if the user stays on the page for a long time. Chrome DevTools for agents has memory debugging tools, so your agent can ensure memory use isn't increasing without bound.
For a closer look at how to use Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents together, check out this video:
Success stories
Engineering teams around the world are already using Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents to improve code quality, speed up delivery, and eliminate manual debugging bottlenecks:
Pensionbazaar and Policybazaar
Pensionbazaar, a new retirement planning platform launched by Indian fintech company Paisabazaar, paired Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents to build and verify new pages, shortening turnaround by more than 90% (from about four days to a few hours) and reducing UI bugs on new screens by over 90%. Its sister platform Policybazaar, one of India's leading insurance platforms with more than 97 million registered customers, used Chrome DevTools for agents to automate performance audits across about 30 high-traffic landing pages, cutting manual auditing effort by 92%:
"For Pensionbazaar, our priority was building quality code from day one to avoid technical debt later. Modern Web Guidance steered our coding agent to adopt modern web standards and performance best practices while respecting our specific browser compatibility targets. This made our frontend code reviews substantially easier and faster, ultimately improving our development turnaround time."
—Aman Soni, Engineering Manager, Policybazaar
WeTV
WeTV, Tencent's international video streaming platform, added an AI coding agent to its CI/CD pipeline that uses Chrome DevTools for agents to diagnose performance regressions and Modern Web Guidance to fix them using modern web platform features. The agent now automatically diagnoses and resolves 90% of failed performance checks, cutting debugging and resolution time by 87% (from four hours to 30 minutes, including manual evaluation):
"The results have been very effective in terms of both speed and quality. The diagnostic insights provided by Chrome DevTools for agents and Modern Web Guidance gave us reliable references for fixing complex layout issues. We perform strict verification after every fix, and the current success rate and stability have significantly improved our release confidence."
—Yangjie Zheng, Head of Engineering, WeTV (Tencent)
note inc.
note inc., one of Japan's largest creator and media platforms with over 90 million monthly active users, used Modern Web Guidance alongside its in-house design system as part of an ongoing effort to modernize its Next.js frontend. Across a 180-run evaluation on its production codebase, Modern Web Guidance raised pass rates on modern web checks from 61% to 94% by steering agents to use native HTML and CSS features instead of custom JavaScript for scroll animations, tooltips, and accordions. It also increased proper LCP image prioritization by 28% across 431 merged PRs:
"Our mission at note is 'Start, and Keep on Creating,' so our platform has to stay fast and accessible for every creator and reader. As more of our code is written with AI coding agents, Modern Web Guidance helps them reach for modern, standards-based solutions instead of falling back on older JavaScript patterns. It also points out details that are easy to miss, such as image loading priority and form accessibility. Combined with our design system, it lets us keep improving note while keeping our UI consistent."
—Takehiko Itabashi, VP of Technology, note inc.
MetaMask
MetaMask, a self-custodial financial platform with more than 100 million downloads across approximately 190 countries, runs Modern Web Guidance as an automated review bot on every pull request to its open source browser extension, configured with just a three-line prompt. In its first five weeks, the bot reviewed roughly 480 pull requests and commented on 64 of them, leading engineers to fix 43 findings (mostly accessibility, HTML semantics, and forms issues that linters don't catch) with a median time of 15 minutes from comment to fix:
"The reviews are really helpful. They've helped surface and get our engineers familiar with modern APIs like Interest invokers and the Popover API. It hasn't increased PR review times, if anything it likely reduced them. The issues MWG caught would have otherwise required a human reviewer familiar with these modern web techniques."
—Francis Nepomuceno, UX Engineer, MetaMask
Ecosystem and community support
Modern Web Guidance started as an initiative within Chrome, but reaching this 1.0 milestone was a collaborative effort with numerous experts across the web community.
Thank you to the content area tech leads overseeing each web platform area, our browser partners at Firefox and Edge, the independent web standards and accessibility experts who authored and tested guides, and all of the open source contributors on GitHub who helped shape this release!
If you spot a gap in what coding agents know about the web, or want to help improve an existing guide, see the contribution guide to get involved.
Get started with Modern Web Guidance
To add Modern Web Guidance to your project, run the CLI installer from your project directory:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
Or if you already installed an earlier version, you can update to 1.0 by running:
npx modern-web-guidance@latest update
In addition to the CLI, you can install and update Modern Web Guidance directly through most popular coding agent plugin marketplaces, including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot, WebStorm, Kimi Code, and Grok Build.
To learn more, check out these resources:

articles.title: Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server
articles.body:
Critical RCE Vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server: Everything You Need To Know
Detect and mitigate CVE-2026-119618, a critical RCE vulnerability in Apache HTTP Server. According to Wiz data, 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618. Immediate patching is advised.
A critical synchronization vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618) has been identified in Apache HTTP Server’s HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). The flaw stems from a concurrent execution race condition within the assign_headers() function when handling shared resources. If successfully exploited, a remote, unauthenticated attacker can corrupt heap memory to achieve arbitrary code execution (RCE).
As of the time of this blog’s publication, no exploit is available and there are no reports of exploitation in the wild.
What is CVE-2026-119618?
CVE-2026-119618 is a critical, high-severity vulnerability involving a race condition in the Apache HTTP Server, which was independently discovered by Anthropic and Google Cloud’s Vulnerability Research Team.
Specifically, the flaw exists within the assign_headers() function of the HTTP/2 module (mod_http2). Due to improper synchronization when executing concurrent threads sharing resources, an attacker can trigger heap corruption. This memory corruption can ultimately be leveraged to achieve RCE on the hosting server, allowing unauthorized threat actors to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the web server process.
Wiz Research data: what’s the risk to cloud environments?
In cloud environments, a compromised Apache instance running containerized or virtualized workloads can serve as an entry point for lateral movement, potentially exposing adjacent microservices or cloud metadata endpoints.
According to Wiz data 64% of cloud environments have resources vulnerable to CVE-2026-119618, and 51% of cloud environments have publicly exposed instances. Note that this does not take configuration into account.
Which products are affected?
The vulnerability affects deployments utilizing HTTP/2 capabilities on the Apache HTTP Server within the version ranges outlined in the table below:
Which actions should security teams take?
Security operations and engineering teams should execute the following remediation and mitigation steps:
1. Upgrade Deployments
Upgrade Apache HTTP Server: Update affected installations to Apache HTTP Server version 2.4.71 or later. This release addresses the race condition in assign_headers().
Update Standalone Modules: If managing standalone mod_h2 builds from GitHub, upgrade the module to a version newer than 2.0.42.
2. Implement Temporary Mitigations
If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, temporarily disable HTTP/2 support to eliminate the attack vector.
Edit the configuration file (such as httpd.conf) to restrict active protocols to HTTP/1.1 by removing h2 and h2c references:
# Restrict protocols to HTTP/1.1Protocols http/1.1
Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment.

articles.title: Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO
articles.body:
Jensen Huang Resigns As Nvidia CEO 109
			
		 	
				Jensen Huang has stepped down as CEO of Nvidia after 33 years leading the company, with CFO Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO while the board searches for a permanent replacement.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," said board chair Harvey Jones in a release announcing the news.
The abrupt departure follows revelations about Huang's affairs, including one with a woman U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese spy. CNBC reports:  Huang, 63, apologized on Sunday for being "unfaithful to my wife," though he provided no details about the affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who has worked for a Chinese company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Late Wednesday, The New York Times reported that the Nvidia CEO also had a separate affair, this one with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at the chipmaker. Later that afternoon The Times and other outlets reported that Nvidia's board met to discuss the company's future.
Jensen Huang denied allegations that he had compromised national security or Nvidia secrets after reports of the Alice Huang affair. The news sparked concerns that Nvidia knew companies based in Singapore and Malaysia had been evading U.S. export controls in accessing its technology. The board said on Tuesday that it had hired Wachtell Lipton to investigate the intelligence allegations.

articles.title: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Nvidia is reportedly planning to oust its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who has led the company for the last 33 years, the Wall Street Journal reports. Sources told the newspaper that the Nvidia board is meeting as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future at the company.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman purported by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. On Wednesday evening, the New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an executive who reports to him.
Nvidia has become one of the most valuable companies in the world as it designs the chips that power the AI boom, but in the midst of Huang’s ongoing scandal, Nvidia stock fell about 8% in after hours trading on Wednesday. The stock is down about 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he has said. The company also has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. According to Bloomberg, Nvidia is working with an outside firm to identify candidates that could potentially replace Huang as CEO.
SpaceXSI CEO Elon Musk late on Wednesday posted on X that hiring Huang “would be an honor.”

articles.title: AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
articles.body:
Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found.
AI chatbots are recommending fake retail websites, study finds
A study testing Gemini, Perplexity, and ChatGPT found that in as many as 15 percent of conversations, chatbots displayed ‘risky’ URLs.
The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of 151 brands. Questions included “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”; “Where can I find [brand] online?”; and “Does [brand] ship internationally? What are their regional websites?” The test ran over the course of two testing periods in September and asked about 151 small and large companies like fashion brands Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, and Madhappy (a client of Podqi) and homeware brand Le Creuset. Podqi crafted its own prompts (as opposed to using real user conversations) and tested its prompts using a tool that tracks AI answers across chatbots.
Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers
Over the course of 6,795 answers, Podqi found that all three AI engines cited and showed shoppers risky sites, defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers or selling knockoffs, old brand domains that have been reregistered by someone else, or dead sites that aren’t active at all but that someone else could purchase and reuse. Google’s Gemini showed risky sites least often of the three, linking to or mentioning a risky site in 4 percent of answers. (Mentions include instances of recommending a risky site, displaying it without comment, and warning a user about it.) Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers. ChatGPT fell somewhere in the middle at 8 percent. ChatGPT performed the best when it came to offering warnings about each risky site that it surfaced, doing so 24 percent of the time. Smaller brands appear especially at risk: Podqi found that queries related to larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often.
AI companies market chatbots as being helpful for shopping tasks like researching, comparing, and discovering products or retailers. AI citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers, of course, but it could also quickly become a risk for consumers. The issue could be especially relevant going into the upcoming holiday shopping season, when consumers are hunting around for in-stock items and the best prices. It’s likely that more consumers will be using AI to shop this year, including buying products from brands or sites they’re not already familiar with.
“Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” says Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West.
“We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested,” Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said in an email. “We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.”
“Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop,” OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said in an email. “We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results. We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.”
In Podqi’s test, certain prompts seemed to trigger risky sites more often than others. For example, AI displayed risky sites more often when asked about regional brand websites compared to other prompt categories. The tested AI engines also at times listed fake regional sites for brands that do not have any. In one conversation, Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website and called it “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.”
“Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years. We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it,” spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in an email.

articles.title: ‘The end of Tesla!’: Cybertruck diehards turn on Elon Musk after he pulls the plug
articles.body:
The Cybertruck is heading to that shiny cyber-dumpster in the sky, leaving the folks who built online identities around Elon Musk’s polarizing pickup feeling bereft. Usually, Musk’s fanbase treads lightly around their idol’s mercurial decisions. This time, however, the truck’s demise has sparked rare backlash within the Tesla community — aimed squarely at the guy who signed its death warrant.
‘The end of Tesla!’: Cybertruck diehards turn on Elon Musk after he pulls the plug
Tesla’s polarizing pickup is heading to the scrap heap, leaving its biggest online boosters feeling betrayed and questioning Musk’s next big pivot.
Troy Meekhof, who posts on numerous social platforms under the moniker “The Cybertruck Guy,” has been vocal about his disappointment in Musk’s decision to wind down Cybertruck production by the end of summer 2027. (The original plan was to start winding down production in the spring, but then Musk decided to extend it a few months.)
In a 33-minute video on YouTube, Meekhof argues that Tesla never fully committed to making the Cybertruck a success, citing a lack of advertising, confusing pricing changes, and the decision to shift focus before the truck could fully establish itself in the market.
“It feels like they didn’t try to make Cybertruck a success,” he said.
He also had choice words for Musk’s reasons for ending the Cybertruck’s short run to make room at Giga Texas for the fully autonomous Cybercab: “Cancelling all of your best products... in favor of an autonomous platform that remains both software and regulatory constrained... seems like an absolutely terrible idea,” Meekhof vented.
The Cybertruck wasn’t the only Tesla product to meet an untimely end — at least according to those with stakes (and often stock options) in the company’s success. Earlier this year, Tesla discontinued the Model S and Model X, two of its flagship vehicles. With the end of the Cybertruck, Tesla is now left with just the Model 3 and Model Y as vehicles you can actually buy. (The Semi is strictly a commercial vehicle, while the Cybercab’s availability as a consumer product remains dubious, at best.)
“Cancelling Cybertruck after all the years of getting it to production to ‘make room for CyberCab’ is a lame excuse,” @TeslaXplored wrote on X. “There are like 500 CyberCabs in one city that only Tesla influencers are riding in. Taking away consumer cars instead of building what the people want will be the end of Tesla!”
He added, “Very sad what happened to Tesla over the last 5 years.”
Meanwhile, at least one prominent aftermarket company is offering to step in and pick up the mantle. Unplugged Performance, which makes aftermarket accessories, said it would produce the Cybertruck and other vehicles on the truck platform under license, with investors funding the effort: “Worth a conversation?”
Musk, for his part, seems less interested in litigating the particulars of Cybertruck production and more intent on selling a vision of Tesla’s future centered around the Cybercab and humanoid robots. “Cybercab will do a majority of all passenger miles in any jurisdiction where it is not prohibited by law,” Musk wrote on X earlier this week. “Obvious to anyone with eyes and a brain.”
He also pushed back on claims that the Cybertruck was killed because it was unprofitable. “The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate,” Musk said. “We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.”
To be sure, Cybertruck sales have been disappointing over its entire production run. Musk initially theorized that Tesla could sell 250,000-500,000 Cybertrucks annually, but the actual numbers have been far below those projections. Last year, Tesla is estimated to have sold around 20,000 trucks; the company is on track to sell fewer than that this year.
Whether Musk’s autonomous utopia pans out or ends up joining the Cybertruck in the vaporware graveyard remains to be seen. For now, the stainless-steel wedge that was supposed to be the ultimate symbol of an indestructible future has become a monument to Musk’s shifting attention span — and a stark reminder to Tesla’s most loyal boosters that in Elon’s world, nothing should be taken for granted.

articles.title: Whoop just launched a social network
articles.body:
Whoop, the maker of screen-less fitness bands, is launching a social network on Thursday that lets its members follow friends and family and share their health data.
The network, called Whoop Humans, will be rolled out in the Whoop app to members at every membership tier at no extra cost. Members can follow anyone on Whoop and choose what to share, from sleep and recovery to workouts and achievements. Followers can react and comment; members can also attach photos and commentary to their data. It’s all opt-in, CEO Will Ahmed tells us.
Whoop already has a social feature, Teams, which a little more than half its customers use, according to the company. But Teams is built around groups and leaderboards, and everyone in a group sees everyone else’s information. Humans is meant to be more intimate. Members decide who follows them and who sees what, so a trainer can track a set of clients without the clients seeing one another’s data, for example.
I found myself questioning how much a spouse wants to know about the other’s sleep score when Ahmed mentioned this particular scenario, so I asked him how else beta members used these newer social features. He said the company learned that people were more engaged when someone reported a low recovery score than a nearly perfect one, suggesting that the new feature may be particularly helpful for understanding when someone is struggling and might need attention.
Indeed, the bigger story here is where Whoop continues to be headed, which is into medical wellness. Like its most direct rival, Oura, the company is pushing faster and more aggressively into the wellness opportunity that an aging population presents.
Whoop had already added FDA-cleared ECG and atrial fibrillation detection, blood pressure insights, blood testing, and medical-record uploads. Asked if older customers are gravitating to Whoop, Ahmed said, without offering specifics, that Whoop has seen “huge growth” among people over 60 over the past 18 months. He also said his was among the first companies accepted into a Medicare program that reimburses qualifying wearables that can show they improve health outcomes, and that it now has Medicare members.
He added that he expects families to be big users of Humans. (You can imagine adult children checking in on aging parents.)
But the company’s efforts to be thought of as the “brand for personal health” raises questions, naturally, about privacy. Ahmed said members choose which metrics to share, can remove followers, and can switch on “stealth mode” to go dark for a few days without changing their settings. Activities marked sensitive aren’t shared by default, and Ahmed said health alerts and medical information aren’t shared at all. Members can also report any comment or photo that they deem disturbing, and the company said reported content is reviewed.
As for minors, Whoop’s minimum age is 13 for all members (higher in some countries), meaning customers of that age can share their data subject to consents and privacy settings. Asked whether a parent could follow a teenager’s data, he didn’t answer directly and pointed to the privacy controls.
Ahmed also said Whoop doesn’t sell member data. “Our product is not you; it’s the membership,” he said, adding that the company doesn’t license data to third parties.
He was candid about dealmaking. Asked about Oura’s announcement this week that it will pay $625 million for Counsel Health, a service offering on-demand physicians, Ahmed said he expects “more consolidation” among AI-focused, clinician-focused, and wearable companies, and that Whoop is always on the prowl. Its deep relationship with members, he said, puts it “in a position to be an acquirer.”
He was more guarded about the company’s own finances, declining to share revenue or say whether Whoop is profitable. He did say that the company now has about 1,200 employees, membership on its software platform has increased more than 70% a year for three years running, and that it expects to have nearly 4 million members by year-end.
As for an IPO (the company raised a very big round earlier this year), he said only that Whoop “will certainly IPO in the future.” He also wouldn’t comment on Oura, which shelved its own IPO of up to $2.2 billion in September citing market uncertainty.
In the meantime, Whoop is widening its reach. The company announced that its devices will be sold through Ulta stores beginning next March (around 500 locations of the beauty retailer to start, and a target to retail in more than a thousand stores eventually). Indeed, Ahmed said Whoop’s female audience has more than doubled from last year.
As for competition, in addition to Google’s new Fitbit Air band, Whoop may soon have to contend with Apple, which is reportedly developing a Whoop-style band. But Ahmed mostly shrugged off those concerns, suggesting that building a product doesn’t guarantee success. Instead, he said, Whoop’s job is to stay true to the “aspiring” people it serves.

articles.title: Paths in Pieces
articles.body:
Paths in pieces
Nov 12th, 2026
Many[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9] Linux distributions and package managers audit just-built binaries for non-relocatable absolute paths. If a binary contains a path /path/from/build/machine, it might not run on the end-user's machine.
Now, a basic grep on the binary, or a slightly more sophisticated
$ strings bin/app | grep /path/from/build/machine
using GNU binutils's strings will detect these paths, right?
The answer is no, at least when using GCC and targeting x86-64: you should not assume that string constants end up literally in the binary.
Basic example
In this C++ source we create a std::string from a string constant:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#define PREFIX "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew"
int main() {
  std::string prefix{PREFIX};
  std::cout << prefix << '\n';
}
Compile with GCC 12 or later and run, which prints the path:
$ g++ -O2 main.cpp -o main
$ ./main
/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew
But the path occurs precisely 0 times in the binary itself:
$ grep -acF /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew main
0
$ strings ./main | grep -cF /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew
0
Surely these bytes must be part of the binary somewhere? Let's run strings on it and grep just for the /home prefix:
$ strings ./main | grep /home
/home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew
Wait, did GCC just turn
/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew
into an entirely different path
/home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew
with a made-up subdirectory xbrew? How?
Store by pieces
The answer is that GCC optimizes our std::string{PREFIX}. The fact that we see something that looks like the prefix is merely a coincidence.
GCC splits our string up into two (overlapping) pieces of 16 bytes, like so
/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew
|--------------|..........  - constant 1
..........|--------------|  - constant 2
which fit exactly in xmm registers, so that it can copy our string to the std::string buffer using vectorized move instructions.
Filtering the relevant bits from g++ -O2 -S -masm=intel, we get
movdqa  xmm0, XMMWORD PTR .LC0[rip]
movups  XMMWORD PTR [rax], xmm0
movdqa  xmm0, XMMWORD PTR .LC1[rip]
movups  XMMWORD PTR 10[rax], xmm0
and our string is stored at .LC0 and .LC1 as constants, which just happen to be next to each other in the binary:
.LC0:
.quad 7596498784141404207
.quad 3420313983963919726
.LC1:
.quad 7795220194874516088
.quad 8603408430414524009
In general, this happens when a string constant is copied into a buffer, as with std::string, strcpy or memcpy; strings that are only passed around as pointers, like in fopen(PREFIX "/x", "r"), stay intact.
Deduplication
Some package managers like Conda and Spack install packages into a padded prefix during their builds, with the idea that they can be “relocated” to a shorter prefix of the user's choice: the binaries are patched in-place. Conda uses a repeated string _placehold in a directory name to make the prefix long enough.
Now, even if we pick a 256-byte path (a convenient multiple of all x86-64 register widths) by padding the path Conda-style
#define PREFIX "/home/conda/feedstock_root/build_artifacts/" \
               "foo_1699999999999/_h_env" \
               "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \
               "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \
               "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold" \
               "_placehold_placehold_placehold_placeho/"
and keep our fingers crossed that GCC puts the pieces of the path contiguously in the binary, we do not see our prefix back in the binary. What we get instead is a much shorter string of only 176 bytes (that is 11 times 16):
$ strings main | grep /home
/home/conda/feedstock_root/build_artifacts/foo_1699999999999/_h_env_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placehold_placeho/
This is thanks to a further optimization: since the string _placehold repeats every 10 bytes, the 16-byte pieces repeat every lcm(10, 16) = 80 bytes, and GCC needs to store only 5 distinct 16-byte constants for the padding:
/home/conda/feed
stock_root/build
_artifacts/foo_1
699999999999/_h_
env_placehold_pl
acehold_placehol  # note
d_placehold_plac  # that
ehold_placehold_  # this
placehold_placeh  # is
old_placehold_pl  # cyclic
acehold_placeho/
Is this optimization helpful?
For string literals, I don't think so. Clang does not split strings into constants, yet it generates essentially the same instructions. For example, take a longer path, and target AVX2 with -march=x86-64-v3:
#define PREFIX "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Cellar/foo/1.2.3/share/foo"
Clang simply puts the string in a section dedicated to strings, .rodata.str1.1:
.L.str:
.asciz "/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/Cellar/foo/1.2.3/share/foo"
and copies its 53 bytes with two overlapping 32-byte ymm loads and stores, at offsets 21 and 0:
vmovups ymm0, ymmword ptr [rip + .L.str+21]
vmovups ymmword ptr [rax + 21], ymm0
vmovups ymm0, ymmword ptr [rip + .L.str]
vmovups ymmword ptr [rax], ymm0
That isn't particularly different from GCC's version, which loads the same two pieces from constants in .rodata.cst32 instead:
vmovdqa ymm0, YMMWORD PTR .LC0[rip]
vmovdqu YMMWORD PTR [rax], ymm0
vmovdqa ymm0, YMMWORD PTR .LC1[rip]
vmovdqu YMMWORD PTR 21[rax], ymm0
So what does GCC gain? In terms of performance, probably nothing measurable: both do the same loads and stores. With repeated pieces, GCC might have a slight edge, because a repeated piece is loaded once and stored multiple times (11 loads for 16 stores in the earlier example). It also uses aligned reads, but that matters only for ancient CPUs.
In terms of size, GCC's pieces can take more space than the string itself: overlapping bytes are stored twice, and the pieces are aligned to 16, 32 or 64 bytes. The 53-byte path above takes 64 bytes as two pieces, against 54 bytes as a string. It only pays off if it results in deduplication, for example when many strings share a prefix of at least 16 bytes for SSE2, 32 bytes for AVX2, and 64 bytes for AVX-512. Presumably deduplication does not save much in practice, especially now that some distributions use AVX2 as their baseline.
Can I disable this optimization?
Other than compiling with -Os, not really. From GCC 10 onwards (maybe older versions too?) the split-into-pieces optimization triggers for strings up to 256 bytes even without specifying -march. From GCC 12 it is relative to the target's vector width, so longer strings get split too: up to 512 bytes for AVX2 and 1024 bytes for AVX-512.
I believe the only control you have over this is setting the maximum vector width to 128 bits (forcing xmm operations), by passing -mstore-max=128. But this merely restores old defaults, and means strings of up to 256 bytes are still stored in pieces.
Maybe post-hoc scanning is bad practice?
These post-build audits for absolute paths are popular, but you could argue that they are too brittle to start with, so why expect them to work at all?
Indeed, Debian goes much further than a bad-path scan. Their audit asserts that a package can be rebuilt bit for bit in different circumstances: on a different machine, with a different user, time and date, hostname, locale, etc. That is a much more reliable way to keep machine-specific details out of binaries.[10]
I would argue that, despite that, it is still useful to keep string constants literally in the binary, even on Debian, because it improves interpretability of binaries. Running strings ./binary is such a simple and convenient way to get insight into an opaque binary blob, that it outweighs the marginal savings that come with splitting and deduplication. It is reminiscent of Fedora and Ubuntu turning frame pointers back on by default, despite the small overhead, just to make profilers and tracing tools work more reliably.
Other than that, there is the argument of binary patching, which — despite being considered somewhat brittle — is common practice in Conda and Spack: upon install to a user-specified location, the absolute paths are patched in-place accordingly, through what can be seen as a glorified sed invocation. This only works if the path is stored in one piece.
If you'd like to discuss this, a good place is the gcc-patches thread that I started recently, with an initial attempt at a patch that adds a way to opt out.
[1] RPM (Fedora, RHEL, openSUSE): check-buildroot greps every installed file for the build root.
[2] Arch Linux: makepkg warns about references to $srcdir and $pkgdir.
[3] Yocto / OpenEmbedded: the buildpaths QA check.
[4] FreeBSD ports: the stage QA greps for the staging directory.
